body.text: In short:
Victoria's Big Build royal commission has referred two witnesses to police for potential prosecution.
The ABC understands a Bandidos bikie and a labour hire boss were referred over allegations they failed to answer the commission's questions.
What's next?
The next block of royal commission hearings will begin on November 30.
The royal commission investigating crime and corruption on Victorian construction sites has referred two witnesses to police for potential prosecution.
The ABC understands Bandidos bikie Joel Leavitt and BK Labour hire boss Bernard Kearney were referred over allegations they failed to answer the commission's questions.
The commission warned in a statement: "As the Commissioner has twice said, the window for early voluntary disclosures is fast closing.

"Anyone who hinders or obstructs the work of the Royal Commission, including witnesses who fail to give honest answers, can expect to be referred to Victoria Police for prosecution for breaches under the Inquiries Act 2014."
Counsel Assisting Chris Carr SC addressed the matter as the commission concluded today's public hearing.

"The commission has today referred a number of matters arising from the evidence of witnesses this week and has referred two people to Victoria Police for consideration of whether they ought to be prosecuted for any offences," he said.
Victoria Police declined to comment.
The commission was due to finish its first block of public hearings tomorrow, but Mr Carr said they were not complete and would instead return later this month.
"This is due to a number of issues, including delays in the production of material and ongoing investigative work," Mr Carr said.
The royal commission confirmed the next block of hearings will take place between November 30 and December 11.
Labour hire company donated thousands of dollars to union
Earlier today, it was revealed a CFMEU-aligned labour hire company brought on to replace another business on a major public project paid thousands in donations to the union.
The union-aligned firm also provided fake invoices to an industry regulator after questions were raised over cash withdrawals and payments to a former top CFMEU official.
BK Labour Hire director Bernard Kearney today concluded his evidence to the royal commission into suspected corruption on Victorian construction projects.
The company had an enterprise bargaining agreement with the CFMEU that helped it get lucrative contracts on Big Build projects beginning around 2022, the commission has been told.
The commission viewed BK Labour bank statements showing thousands of dollars in donations directly to the CFMEU or union-linked entities.
"Did you think the union was a charity?" commissioner Chris Kourakis asked.
"I actually can't remember," Mr Kearney replied.
Circumstances probed around stoppage at Sunbury project
BK Labour Hire was taken on as a subcontractor on a level crossing removal project at Gap Road in Sunbury, north-west of Melbourne, in June 2022.

The commission is probing the circumstances around a two-day work stoppage on the project, on June 6 and 7, which resulted in CFMEU-aligned contractors and health and safety representatives being brought onto the project.
BK Labour was one of the firms brought on to replace another firm that did not have an enterprise bargaining agreement with the union.

Mr Kearney admitted it was unusual and disruptive for labour hire to change on a project midway through and said he assumed the change was something to do with a dispute between the CFMEU and John Holland.
However, BK Labour general manager Duane Allen said he did not question why the company was being sought to take over on the project, calling it a "stroke of luck".
"What's happening is you're being put on this job by the CFMEU," counsel assisting the commission Chris Carr suggested.
"No," Mr Allen replied.
The commission was shown a $5,000 donation from BK Labour hire paid on June 7, 2022 — the same day the Gap Road dispute was resolved — listed as being to the Port Melbourne Football Club.
Mr Kearney said he did not have any knowledge of the payment to the club, which has been sponsored by the CFMEU, or what it was for.
"Did you have any relationship with Port Melbourne FC?" he was asked.
Mr Kearney replied: "I can't remember."
Kearney willing to 'take the rap' for fake invoice requests

BK Labour Hire came under scrutiny from industry regulator the Labour Hire Authority in September 2025 over cash withdrawals totalling $77,970 and transfers to various entities in the name of former senior CFMEU organiser Joe Myles, totalling $127,472.
Rather than provide a statutory declaration explaining the transactions as requested by the regulator, Mr Kearney admitted to requesting fake invoices be made up.
"I'll take the rap for that, yep," he said.
However, Mr Kearney maintained Mr Myles was paid through his companies for work he had done, describing him as an asset for his knowledge of health and safety procedures.
"Why didn't you just reply to the Labor Hire Authority and tell them that?" Mr Kourakis asked.
"Honestly, Commissioner, I can't answer that," Mr Kearney replied.
BK Labour received a succession of invoices from Mr Myles totalling $256,000 over about a year, the commission heard yesterday.
Mr Myles was sacked by the union in mid-2024.
Yesterday, Mr Kearney was also grilled over $165,000 the company paid to union-aligned Bandidos gang member Joel Leavitt.
Mr Kearney admitted Mr Leavitt had not provided any work for the firm but said he had "just decided to pay it and move on".
"I can't answer why," he said.
With AAP
